newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: ASEAN ministers to meet on Cambodia - Malaysia.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN ministers to meet on Cambodia - Malaysia.

text.p: Foreign Ministers of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) will meet in Kuala Lumpur on Thursday to discuss the crisis in Cambodia, the Malaysian news agency Bernama reported on Monday.

The news agency quoted Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi as saying in Croatia that ministers of the seven-member grouping were in touch with each other on Monday and decided to meet in Kuala Lumpur.
Abdullah, who is visiting the Balkans, said ASEAN would issue a statement in Kuala Lumpur on Tuesday about the strife in Cambodia.
Malaysia is the current chairman of ASEAN, which also groups Indonesia, Brunei, the Philippines, Singapore, Vietnam and Thailand.
Cambodia, which was plunged into turmoil following two days of fighting in the capital Phnom Penh over the weekend, was to join ASEAN later this month along with Burma and Laos.
Badawi in his comments to Bernama did not indicate whether ASEAN would reconsider plans to admit its last three members as a group at the annual ASEAN meetings.
But Philippines Foreign Minister Domingo Siazon said that was a distinct possibility.

"If this fighting does not stop, obviously ASEAN members will have to rethink this seriously...because they may not be capable of dealing with the situation of war inside the country," Siazon told reporters on Monday.
"If the situation requires, we will have to review the decision of the foreign ministers with respect to membership," Siazon said.
Second Prime Minister Hun Sen has taken control of Phnom Penh and its outskirts, while his ousted rival, Prince Norodom Ranariddh, has vowed from France to organise resistance.
Squeezed between Thailand and Vietnam with China as an interested party, Cambodia has strategic significance in the region.
ASEAN has long been involved in efforts to end the country's seemingly insurmountable factional conflict.

Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas played a key role in the Paris Peace accords that led to U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993 and the political chimera of a country ruled by two prime ministers who are sworn enemies.

The Paris accords were meant to end a civil war that began with the 1970 overthrow of the U.S.-backed Lon Nol government and descended into savagery with the 1975-79 "killing fields" regime of Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge.

Vietnam invaded in 1979 to oust Pol Pot and installed a pro-Hanoi regime under Hun Sen. ASEAN defined itself in the 1980s by opposing the Hun Sen government and supporting an anti-Vietnamese guerrilla coalition that included Ranariddh's royalists and the Khmer Rouge.
